title: I'm Waiting for the Man
recordingNote: Recorded May 1966 at TTG Studios, Hollywood; official Universal Music Group audio from The Velvet Underground & Nico 45th Anniversary (Super Deluxe Edition)
context: Recorded in May 1966 at TTG Studios in Hollywood and released on Verve on 12 March 1967, this is Lou Reed's unsentimental story of riding the subway to Harlem to buy heroin — a plain-spoken drug song on a major label, with Andy Warhol credited as producer. Critics file it among the founding documents of proto-punk, a garage-rock stomper years ahead of the punk wave it helped start.
listenFor: The relentless piano vamp hammering away under Reed's deadpan vocal, never once resolving into a chorus.

title: "Heroes"
recordingNote: Recorded July–August 1977 at Hansa by the Wall, West Berlin; official HD video from David Bowie's channel (2018)
context: Written with Brian Eno and produced by Bowie and Tony Visconti, "Heroes" was recorded in July and August 1977 at Hansa Studios in West Berlin, close to the Wall, and released as a single on 23 September 1977. The album version stretches past six minutes; the single was trimmed to 3:32 — a love song shot through the cold of the city's divided, art-rock years.
listenFor: Bowie's voice climbing an octave higher with each repeat of "I, I will be king".

title: London Calling
recordingNote: From the December 1979 double album London Calling; official video on the theclashVEVO channel (2009 upload)
context: The Clash's apocalyptic opener was recorded at Wessex Studios in a former church hall in North London and released as a single on 7 December 1979, ahead of the double album of the same name. Its title echoes the BBC World Service announcement "This is London calling", and its ice-age imagery was partly spurred by the March 1979 Three Mile Island nuclear accident. It reached No. 11 in the UK and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2007.
listenFor: Paul Simonon's descending bass line pulling the song in before Strummer's hoarse warning arrives.

title: Where Is My Mind?
recordingNote: Original recording 1988 on Surfer Rosa; official 4AD audio upload (the Death to the Pixies compilation version)
context: The closing track on Surfer Rosa, the Pixies' 1988 debut album, "Where Is My Mind?" became the band's signature song after its use in the 1999 film Fight Club brought it a second life. It has since drawn a multitude of covers and turned up across film, television and games, outgrowing every other song in the Boston band's catalogue.
listenFor: The woozy lead guitar wandering off-key while Kim Deal's backing "oohs" circle the chorus.

title: Paranoid Android
recordingNote: Lead single from OK Computer, released 26 May 1997 on Parlophone; official video on Radiohead's channel (2015 upload)
context: Six and a half minutes and four distinct sections, released as the lead single from OK Computer on 26 May 1997 — "Paranoid Android" took its title from Marvin in The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, its lyrics from a hostile night Thom Yorke experienced in a Los Angeles bar. It reached No. 3 in the UK, and Magnus Carlsson's surreal animated video got heavy MTV rotation.
listenFor: The gear-change when Jonny Greenwood's guitar solo erupts after the second "rain down" section.

title: Seven Nation Army
recordingNote: Lead single from Elephant, released 17 February 2003 on V2/XL; official video on The White Stripes channel (2008 upload)
context: Jack White sketched the famous riff at a soundcheck at Melbourne's Corner Hotel in January 2002, playing a semi-acoustic guitar through an octave pedal — there is no bass guitar anywhere on the recording. Released 17 February 2003 as the lead single from Elephant, it won the 2004 Grammy for Best Rock Song and became a global sports anthem, especially around the 2018 World Cup.
listenFor: The growling octave-pedal riff standing alone at the start until the drums crash in behind it.

title: Rebellion (Lies)
composer: Win Butler, Régine Chassagne, Tim Kingsbury, Richard Reed Parry & Howard Bilerman
recordingNote: From Funeral, released 14 September 2004 on Merge Records; official remastered video on ArcadeFireVEVO (2019 upload)
context: From Funeral, Arcade Fire's debut album — released through Merge Records on 14 September 2004, shadowed by the deaths of several band members' relatives during its making — "Rebellion (Lies)" followed as its fourth single on 12 September 2005. It outdid the album's other singles in the UK, reaching No. 19, and has become the band's most-performed live song.
listenFor: The driving piano figure and Régine Chassagne's wordless high vocal pushing the song toward its final surge.

title: Do I Wanna Know?
recordingNote: Lead single from AM, released on Domino in June 2013; official video on the Arctic Monkeys channel
context: David Wilson's animated video for "Do I Wanna Know?" went up on YouTube on 18 June 2013 and had passed a billion views by June 2020 — one of only twelve rock videos to get there. It introduced Arctic Monkeys' fifth album, AM, released later that year on Domino, with James Ford and Ross Orton producing Alex Turner's turn toward slow-burn, heavy-groove songwriting.
listenFor: The woozy lead-guitar line that answers Turner's opening question like a second voice.

title: Masseduction
recordingNote: Title track of MASSEDUCTION, released 13 October 2017 on Loma Vista; official video on St. Vincent's channel (2019 upload)
context: The title track of St. Vincent's fifth album, MASSEDUCTION, made with producer Jack Antonoff and released on Loma Vista on 13 October 2017, "Masseduction" won Best Rock Song at the 2019 Grammy Awards. Annie Clark framed the record around what she called "sex and drugs and sadness", and it became her first US top-ten album, reaching No. 10 on the Billboard 200.
listenFor: Clark's electric-guitar solo slicing through the glossy synth-pop sheen near the end.

title: Starburster
recordingNote: Lead single from Romance, released 17 April 2024 on XL Recordings; official video on the Fontaines DC channel
context: Fontaines D.C. released "Starburster" on 17 April 2024 as the lead single from Romance, their fourth album and first for XL Recordings. Frontman Grian Chatten wrote it in the grip of a panic attack suffered at London's St Pancras station, and the track's gasping intake of breath drives its hip-hop-adjacent rhythm. It became the Irish band's first UK charting single, peaking at No. 57.
listenFor: The sharp gasp of breath that opens the track and keeps returning like a skipped heartbeat.
